thread.title: Stocks Rise, as Trade and Tech Remain Familiar Refrains

author: Ben Levisohn
title: Stocks Rise, as Trade and Tech Remain Familiar Refrains
text:
President Trump was reported to be in favor of placing tariffs on $200 billion of Chinese goods. Photo: BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/AFP/Getty Images By Ben Levisohn Aug. 31, 2018 8:17 p.m. ET The market’s always changing—but some things about it never change.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 174.47 points, or 0.7%, to 25,964.82 last week, while the S&P 500 gained 0.9%, to 2901.52. The Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.1%, to 8109.54. But at one point, the gains looked like they could be so much better than that.
From Monday through Wednesday, the S&P and the Nasdaq Composite reached all-time highs after the U.S. and Mexico agreed on new trade rules that could replace the North American Free Trade Agreement, and investors started to price out some of the worst trade fears. Those concerns weren’t going to go away that easily, though. On Thursday, President Donald Trump was reported to be in favor of placing tariffs on $200 billion of Chinese goods, which caused the S&P 500 to drop 0.4%.
Still, there’s no denying that investors are willing to pay up for the market. The S&P 500 closed the week trading at 16.8 times 12-month forward earnings, according to Bloomberg data, up from 16.2 times at the end of June.
Savita Subramanian, chief U.S. equity strategist at Bank of America Merrill Lynch, credits the easing of trade tensions around Nafta for the rise in the S&P 500’s valuation. “With the recent symbolic agreement between the U.S. and Mexico, some of the overhang of trade friction has been removed,” Subramanian writes. “Nafta-sensitive segments, as well as the overall S&P 500, have begun rerating as trade agreements reduce uncertainty.”
That uncertainty increased toward the end of the week, however, as it appeared that the U.S. and Canada would head into the weekend without a deal. And investors seem to have approached it the same way they have for much of the past five years—by buying the extended FAANMGs family. Apple (AAPL) and Microsoft (MSFT) were the two best-performing stocks in the Dow Jones Industrial Average last week, while Amazon.com (AMZN) crossed the $2,000 threshold and approached a $1 trillion market value.
More in Trader Best Buy Can’t Get No Respect That is both the good and bad news. Just a few weeks ago, investors were wondering if the run in Facebook (FB), Netflix (NFLX), and other hot tech stocks was over. It’s not, if last week is anything to go by. At the same time, it reinforces the view that tech is the place to be.
Indeed, Frank Gretz, a technical analyst at Wellington Shields, observes that stocks like Autodesk (ADSK), Arista Networks (ANET), and Splunk (SPLK) have also been rallying this month on good news, and in the process have created a market that looks a lot like the Nifty Fifty of the 1960s, when the way to win was by owning just 50 stocks.

It might still happen.
